passage:
(Tanuja, on the bus home from the interview)
Tanuja: they offered 22k a month for the physics batches
Zeenat: ooh! taking it?
Tanuja: my first thought was ask for 25. then i caught myself
Tanuja: 25 only feels right bc they said 22
Zeenat: meaning?
Tanuja: if nobody had said any number, what would i ask? no idea honestly
Tanuja: so i'm asking around first
Tanuja: messaged 3 people. Rukhsar at the other centre gets 30. Deepti's institute pays 28 for 2 batches. the govt tuition scheme is 26 plus travel
Zeenat: so 22 is low 😮
Tanuja: yep. i'll ask for 30 and explain the batch sizes
Zeenat: proud of you, madam 😄
Tanuja: also scared lol. but it's my number now, not theirs

qa.q: How much does Rukhsar get at the other centre?
qa.a: Rukhsar at the other centre gets 30.

qa.q: Why does Tanuja say it's "my number now, not theirs"?
qa.a: She has built her figure from three outside comparisons, so she feels it rests on real information instead of on the 22 they said first. That gives her confidence even though she is still scared.

qa.q: What was the key moment that changed how Tanuja approached the offer?
qa.a: When she noticed 25 only felt right because they said 22, and asked what she would judge with no number at all. That led her to gather comparisons before answering.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see Tanuja by the end of the chat?
qa.a: Zeenat seems impressed and proud, calling her "madam," and may also learn to ask around before accepting a first figure.

grounding: A young woman notices a salary offer is steering her, asks what she would judge without it, and collects three independent comparisons.

passage: At the Thursday haat in Pipariya, Lakshmi stood before the trader's two goats with her self-help group's money tied in her dupatta. "Eighteen thousand for the pair," the trader said, "and I'm giving you a good rate." Lakshmi felt her mind start to bargain from there: sixteen, maybe fifteen. She stopped. If he hadn't said eighteen, what would she think these goats were worth? She didn't know. "I'll come back," she said. Her friend Sangeeta raised an eyebrow. "He might sell them." "Then he sells them." Together they walked the rows. A man near the banyan tree was asking eleven for a similar pair. Sangeeta's cousin, who kept goats in the next village, said on the phone that ten to twelve was fair this season. Lakshmi went back with her own figure. She bought the pair for twelve.

qa.q: How much did the trader first ask for the pair of goats?
qa.a: Eighteen thousand for the pair.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi say "I'll come back" even though the goats might be sold?
qa.a: She realised her bargaining was starting from the trader's eighteen, not from any real knowledge. She preferred to risk losing the goats than to spend the group's money on his number.

qa.q: Which step made Lakshmi's final price fair?
qa.a: Getting two separate comparisons, the man near the banyan tree and Sangeeta's cousin, before going back. That gave her a figure that did not depend on the first price.

qa.q: How might the other women in Lakshmi's self-help group feel about how she spent their money?
qa.a: They would likely trust her more, since she saved thousands by checking prices rather than accepting a trader's opening figure.

grounding: At a village market, a young woman stops bargaining from a trader's first price, asks what she would judge without it, and checks two other prices.

passage:
"Zainab, come see! Pepper learned to sit!"
"No, Aditi baji. I'm staying on the sofa."
"She's a puppy. She's this big."
"Rehan in my class said a dog bit his neighbour's leg and he needed injections. Dogs bite."
Aditi's mother came in with a plate of pakoras. "Zainab, how many dogs do you know?"
Zainab thought. "Pepper. Nanu's dog. The shop dog. The white one at school."
"Have any of them bitten anyone?"
"...No. But Rehan's story."
"One story is very loud, isn't it?" said Aditi's mother. "It shouts over all the quiet ones."
Pepper wobbled over and sniffed Zainab's sock. Zainab pulled her feet up fast. Then, very slowly, she put one finger down. Pepper licked it.
"Eww," said Zainab. But she didn't pull back.

qa.q: What trick had Pepper learned?
qa.a: Pepper learned to sit.

qa.q: Why does it feel true to Zainab that dogs bite?
qa.a: Rehan's story about the bite was scary and easy to remember, so it seemed like what dogs usually do. The many dogs she knows that never bit anyone didn't come to mind.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make at the end, and why was it a good small step?
qa.a: She slowly put one finger down for Pepper. Testing the fear a little at a time let a real, gentle dog start to outweigh the scary story.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel when Zainab refuses to meet Pepper?
qa.a: Aditi is probably disappointed, since she was excited to show off the new puppy, and may want her cousin to see how gentle Pepper is.

grounding: A young girl hears one scary dog-bite story and decides all dogs bite, even a small puppy at her cousin's home.

passage: I'm Vaibhav, and as a boy of nine I feared every dog in the world. It started when my cousin Indu told me about a boy at her school who got bitten by a stray. She did the growl and the scream. After that, I saw that bite whenever I saw a dog. I crossed the road when I saw Bholu, our neighbour's old dog, though he just sleeps by the gate and had licked my hand a hundred times. I told Ma, "All dogs bite, it's true, Indu said." Ma asked, "How many dogs have bitten you?" None. I still didn't pat Bholu for a long time. Now I do. He's very soft. And Indu admits she made the growl louder than it was.

qa.q: What was the name of the neighbour's old dog?
qa.a: Bholu.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav cross the road even to avoid Bholu?
qa.a: Indu's dramatic story with the growl and the scream was so vivid that it came to mind every time he saw any dog. It felt more real than all the times Bholu had licked his hand.

qa.q: What question from Ma could help Vaibhav, and how might he use it next time?
qa.a: "How many dogs have bitten you?" Next time a scary story makes him afraid, he can count what has really happened to him before deciding something is always true.

qa.q: How might Indu feel knowing her story scared Vaibhav for so long?
qa.a: She might feel a bit guilty, which is why she now admits she made the growl louder than it was.

grounding: A boy recalls how one vivid bite story from his cousin made him fear every dog, even a gentle old neighbour's dog.

passage: Tanuja, beti, you're sixteen now and laughing at yourself, but let your Zeenat Nani remind you of last winter. You'd been watching those short clips every night, auto-rickshaws tipping over, bikes skidding, one after another. And suddenly Lucknow was the most dangerous city on earth. You wouldn't take the shared auto to tuition. You wanted your abbu to drive you, both ways, every day. I asked you, "How many of your friends have been in an accident?" You said, "Nani, you don't understand, I see it every day." And that was it, you see? You saw it every day, on the phone. Not on the road. Your abbu and I, we've taken autos for thirty years. Then your teacher showed your class real road figures for our district, and your face changed. You took the auto the next Monday, holding my hand very tight.

qa.q: What did Tanuja want her abbu to do every day?
qa.a: She wanted her abbu to drive her to tuition, both ways, every day.

qa.q: Why did Lucknow suddenly feel so dangerous to Tanuja last winter?
qa.a: She watched accident clips every night, so crashes felt like they were happening all the time. Seeing them so often on the phone felt like proof they were common on the road.

qa.q: What was the turning point that helped Tanuja take the auto again?
qa.a: Her teacher showed the class real road figures for their district. Comparing the numbers with the flood of clips helped her see the difference.

qa.q: How might Zeenat Nani have felt when Tanuja held her hand so tightly on that Monday?
qa.a: She was probably touched and proud that her granddaughter was facing the fear, while still gently holding her through it. 🤍

grounding: A grandmother recalls how accident clips seen every night made her teenage granddaughter believe city travel was far riskier than it was.

passage: The application for the summer science programme in Mumbai closed at midnight, and at 10:40 Farida still hadn't pressed submit. The power had gone at nine, and her laptop was at 14 percent. Nandini sat beside her with a torch. "What's the problem? You've wanted this all year." Farida scrolled on her phone instead. "Look. People packed on local trains. Someone falling off at a station. A building collapse. Floods. My feed is full of it. Mumbai is just unsafe." "How many of those clips are from this year?" "I don't know. Lots." "My cousin lived there two years," Nandini said. "She took the train daily. The worst thing that happened was a stolen umbrella." Farida went quiet. "It feels like it happens every day." "It happens every day on your phone." At 11:52, the laptop at 4 percent, Farida pressed submit.

qa.q: What time did the application close?
qa.a: It closed at midnight.

qa.q: Why does Mumbai feel "just unsafe" to Farida?
qa.a: Her feed is full of dramatic clips about trains, collapses and floods, so it feels like these things happen constantly. Seeing them often is mistaken for them being common.

qa.q: With the battery running out, what helped Farida make her choice?
qa.a: Nandini asked how many clips were recent and shared her cousin's real experience of daily train travel. Comparing the feed with an actual life gave Farida enough balance to press submit.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini to watch Farida nearly miss the deadline?
qa.a: Nandini is probably anxious and a bit frustrated, knowing how much Farida wanted this, which is why Nandini keeps asking calm, clear questions. 😬

grounding: A teenager nearly skips a Mumbai programme because her feed of disaster clips makes the city seem far riskier than it is.

passage:
Hi Maria,
Goa was lovely, but I have to confess something funny, or maybe not funny.
You know that shark video that went round last month, the one from Australia? I watched it maybe ten times. So when everyone went swimming at Palolem, I stayed on the sand. I told them I had a cold. I couldn't stop picturing a fin.
But here's the thing. Every day I rented a scooter and rode to the beach without a helmet, hair flying, feeling free. I didn't think twice. Then on the last day a local boy skidded on sand right in front of me. He was okay, just scraped. I was shaking for an hour.
I've been wondering which thing I should actually have been scared of.
Write soon,
Dilnaz

qa.q: Where did everyone go swimming while Dilnaz stayed on the sand?
qa.a: At Palolem.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz feel more afraid of sharks than of riding without a helmet?
qa.a: The shark video was dramatic and replayed many times, so the danger felt huge and close. Riding the scooter felt normal and free, so its much more common risk hardly came to mind.

qa.q: After seeing the boy skid, what choice could Dilnaz make on the next trip?
qa.a: Dilnaz could wear a helmet on every ride and, before avoiding something scary, ask how often it really happens compared with everyday risks.

qa.q: How might Maria react to reading this letter?
qa.a: Maria might smile at the shark story but feel worried about the helmet part, and glad that Dilnaz is starting to question which fear makes sense.

grounding: A student writes that a viral shark video kept the writer out of the sea, while the same writer rode a scooter daily without a helmet.

passage: You asked why I won't take the room on the ninth floor, Ujjwal? Okay. Since that documentary on the earthquake in Turkey, I can't stop thinking about it. The buildings folding, people under the rubble. I've watched clips every night for two weeks. I told the hostel office I'd only take a ground-floor room. They think I'm mad. What? The scooter? That's different. Yes, I ride to college without a helmet, but it's just ten minutes. Everybody does it. It messes up my hair. ...Why are you making that face? You think the scooter is more dangerous? That's not the same thing at all. An earthquake is, like, huge. I'm Parveen, I'm doing a science degree, I know how to think about risk. ...Okay, fine. Show me the numbers, then. But I'm still not taking the ninth floor.

qa.q: Which room did Parveen refuse to take?
qa.a: The room on the ninth floor.

qa.q: Why does Parveen think the scooter is "different" from an earthquake?
qa.a: The earthquake images are huge and frightening and Parveen has watched them every night, so that danger fills Parveen's mind. The daily scooter ride feels ordinary and short, so its risk seems small.

qa.q: What choice could Parveen make after Ujjwal shows the numbers?
qa.a: Parveen could start wearing a helmet on the daily ride even while still nervous about high floors, putting caution where the more common risk is.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel listening to Parveen argue about risk?
qa.a: Ujjwal may be amused but also worried, and is trying to get Parveen to look at real numbers without mocking the fear.

grounding: A student afraid of high floors after earthquake coverage talks about riding a scooter daily without a helmet as if it were safe.

passage: The rumour reached the village near Chitradurga by phone on a Tuesday: men in a white van were taking children from the fields. By evening Sahil's mother had locked the gate at five, and his aunt refused to let the children walk to the anganwadi. Sahil, holding his three-month-old daughter on the verandah, listened to the relatives on speaker. Everyone had forwarded the same message; no one knew where it came from. He looked around his own house. The kerosene tin by the stove. The old well behind the cowshed with a broken lid. His wife, Keerthana, said quietly, "The well frightens me more than any van." The next day Sahil went to the police outpost and asked if there had been any such case in the district. "None," the constable said. "Same message every monsoon." That afternoon, Sahil fixed the well lid.

qa.q: What did the rumour say was happening in the fields?
qa.a: Men in a white van were taking children from the fields.

qa.q: What was Sahil probably thinking as he looked around his own house?
qa.a: He was likely worried and starting to see that the real risks for his baby might be close at home, like the kerosene tin and the well, not the van in the forwarded message.

qa.q: Which choice by Sahil made his daughter safer?
qa.a: Checking the rumour at the police outpost instead of passing it on, and then fixing the broken well lid, a real everyday danger.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Sahil fixes the lid?
qa.a: She would likely feel heard and relieved, since she had said the well frightened her more than any van. 🙂

grounding: A new father in a village notices relatives panic over a forwarded kidnapping rumour, checks with the police, and fixes a real risk at home.

passage: In their Prague flat, Pavel was changing his son's nappy when his phone buzzed again. Jana's sister Camila had forwarded a message to the family group: strangers were snatching babies from prams in the city parks. "Don't take Matěj out alone!" By noon Jana's mother had called twice. Jana looked shaken. "Maybe we just stay in this week." Pavel wiped his hands and read the message again. No names, no dates, no source. He searched the police website: no reports of any such thing. Then he glanced around the room. The car seat they still hadn't fitted properly. The blind cord hanging near the cot. "I'm not saying we shouldn't be careful," he told Jana. "I'm saying let's be careful about the real stuff." That evening, instead of replying to the group, he fitted the car seat and tied up the cord.

qa.q: What did Camila's forwarded message claim?
qa.a: Strangers were snatching babies from prams in the city parks.

qa.q: Why might Jana want to stay in all week?
qa.a: The message was frightening and everyone in the family was repeating it, so the danger felt close and real. As a new parent, Jana wanted to protect Matěj from anything that might happen.

qa.q: What did Pavel do that was wiser than replying to the group?
qa.a: He checked the police website, found no reports, and then dealt with the car seat and blind cord, the risks actually in their home.

qa.q: How might Camila feel if she learned Pavel had checked the police website?
qa.a: Camila might feel a bit embarrassed for forwarding a false message, but also relieved that nothing like it was happening.

grounding: A new father abroad sees relatives panic over a forwarded baby-snatching message, checks the police site, and fixes real risks at home.

passage:
Monday. At lunch, Kashish told a gripping story about a cousin's kitchen: the gas cylinder hissing, flames up the wall, everyone running. Avni went home and stared at her own stove. She searched induction cooktops and nearly spent twelve thousand before dinner.
Wednesday. The story still made her stomach tighten. But Avni made herself stop and ask: how often does this actually happen? She opened the state fire service's yearly report and the gas company's safety page. Cylinder fires were rare, and most had one thing in common: old, cracked rubber pipes and no regular checks.
Saturday. The gas company's mechanic came to Avni's flat and replaced her pipe, which was five years old. She kept her stove. On her fridge she stuck a note: "Scary story? Check how often first." Kashish, visiting later, read it and laughed. "Was that about me?" "A little," Avni said.

qa.q: What did the gas company's mechanic replace on Saturday?
qa.a: Her pipe, which was five years old.

qa.q: Why did Avni nearly buy an induction cooktop on Monday?
qa.a: Kashish's story was vivid and frightening, so a gas fire suddenly felt likely in her own kitchen. Buying something new felt like a quick way to feel safe.

qa.q: What was Avni's turning point on Wednesday, and what did it change?
qa.a: She paused to ask how often such fires really happen and read reliable reports. That showed her the actual risk was an old pipe, so she fixed that instead of replacing the stove.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel on reading the note on the fridge?
qa.a: Kashish seems amused rather than hurt, and may realise how powerful a dramatic story can be for the listener.

grounding: A young woman pauses after a vivid gas-fire story, looks up how often it really happens, and fixes the actual risk instead of panicking.

passage: Mehak, you want to stop taking the night bus because of that video? Sit with your masi a minute. When I was twenty-four and new in Bengaluru, someone at work told a story about a robbery on the late train. Knives, a woman's chain snatched, the whole compartment screaming. It was all anyone talked about for a week. I stopped taking the train home. I spent half my salary on cabs. I lay awake thinking about knives. Then one Sunday I told myself, "Disha, you're an engineer. Find out how often this happens." I looked up the railway police's yearly figures and asked two women who'd done that route for years. It was rare, and one story had been repeated a hundred times. I went back to the train, sat in the ladies' coach near the guard, and kept my chain inside my kurta. So look it up first, beta. Then decide.

qa.q: What did Disha spend half her salary on?
qa.a: She spent half her salary on cabs.

qa.q: Why did Disha lie awake thinking about knives?
qa.a: The robbery story was dramatic and everyone kept repeating it, so it felt as if it could happen on any train. The vivid picture made the danger feel far more common than it was.

qa.q: What choice did Disha make on that Sunday, and how did it change her habit?
qa.a: She decided to find out how often such robberies really happened, using railway police figures and two regular commuters. Knowing it was rare, she went back to the train with sensible precautions.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel hearing that Disha Masi once did the same thing?
qa.a: Mehak may feel less silly about being scared and more willing to check the facts before giving up the night bus.

grounding: An aunt tells Mehak how she once gave up the train after a vivid robbery story, then checked reliable figures and returned with sensible care.

passage: On day one of the summer chess camp at the community centre, the coach said, "Pick a partner for the puzzle relay." Nilesh, eight, didn't hesitate. He walked straight to Tarun, a thin, quiet boy with big round glasses who was reading the rules sheet. "He looks like a topper," Nilesh whispered to himself. Sonu, a loud boy who had been bouncing a ball, came up hopefully. Nilesh shook his head. "You're too noisy for chess." The relay began. Tarun stared at the first puzzle for ages and got it wrong. At the next table, Sonu shouted "Checkmate!" and slammed down the knight, the fastest in the room. Nilesh's mouth dropped open. At lunch, he went and sat next to Sonu. "How did you see that knight move?"

qa.q: How did Sonu's pair do in the relay?
qa.a: Sonu shouted "Checkmate!" and was the fastest in the room.

qa.q: Why was Nilesh so sure Tarun would be good at chess?
qa.a: Tarun was quiet, read the rules and wore big round glasses, which matched Nilesh's picture of a topper. The look felt like enough proof.

qa.q: What choice did Nilesh make at lunch, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: He sat next to Sonu and asked how he saw the knight move. That let him learn about Sonu from what Sonu actually did, not from how loud he was.

qa.q: How might Sonu have felt when Nilesh said he was too noisy for chess?
qa.a: Sonu probably felt hurt and left out, being judged before playing a single move.

grounding: A boy at chess camp picks a quiet boy with glasses as his partner because he looks clever, and refuses a loud boy who turns out to be the best.

passage: I'm Nandini, and I help run the Sunday maths club in our building's hall. Here's what I saw with Farida, who's ten. We were forming teams for the number puzzles. Farida marched up to Pranit, who wears thick glasses and barely speaks, and said, "You're with me." Then Gogi, who is loud and was doing cartwheels near the door, asked to join. Farida said, "No thanks, you'll just mess around." I don't know exactly what was in her head. But she kept glancing at Pranit's glasses like they were a guarantee. In the round, Pranit froze; he'd never done this kind of puzzle. Gogi, on another team, finished first and whooped. Farida went red. Later I saw her ask Gogi to show her his trick. Maybe she learned something.

qa.q: What was Gogi doing near the door when he asked to join?
qa.a: He was doing cartwheels near the door.

qa.q: Why might Farida have thought Pranit was a guarantee?
qa.a: He looked like her idea of a clever child, with thick glasses and a quiet manner, so choosing him felt safe. Gogi's loudness seemed to mean he would not be serious.

qa.q: After the round, what did Farida choose to do, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She asked Gogi to show her his trick. That shows she was willing to learn from what she saw rather than stick to her first guess.

qa.q: How might Pranit feel being picked because of his glasses?
qa.a: Pranit may feel pressure to be a genius and embarrassed when he freezes, since he had never done this kind of puzzle.

grounding: A maths club helper describes a girl at a maths club who picks a quiet boy with glasses as her partner and turns away a loud boy who then wins.

passage:
Teacher's note: Class 9 chemistry, practical lab, 12 August. Written by Nikita Sharma.
Today I let students pick lab partners for the titration practical. Gautam, usually thoughtful, avoided Birsa, the tall boy who joined on the sports quota. I heard Gautam tell his friend, "He's a footballer, he won't know titration." He chose the student with the neatest notebook instead. During the practical, Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times. Birsa and his partner got a clean result on the first try, and Birsa explained the colour change to the next table. Gautam watched with his mouth half open. After class he came to my desk and said, "Ma'am, I thought he'd be bad at this. I was wrong." We talked about how he had decided before seeing any evidence. Next week I'll rotate partners at random, and I've asked Gautam to work with Birsa.

qa.q: What happened to Gautam's pair during the practical?
qa.a: Gautam's pair overshot the end point three times.

qa.q: Why did it seem sensible to Gautam that Birsa wouldn't know titration?
qa.a: Birsa was tall and joined on the sports quota, which fit Gautam's idea of a footballer, not a chemist. The match to a type felt like enough reason.

qa.q: What did Nikita decide to do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: She will rotate partners at random and has asked Gautam to work with Birsa, so Gautam can learn about Birsa from real work instead of assumptions.

qa.q: What might it be like for Birsa to be overlooked as a lab partner?
qa.a: Birsa may be used to people assuming sports is all he is good at, and explaining the colour change to the next table may have felt like a quiet way of proving otherwise.

grounding: A teacher notes that a teenage boy avoided a sports-quota classmate as a lab partner, assuming he'd be weak, and was surprised by his skill.

passage:
Friday, 9 pm
Diary, I owe someone an apology, but only in here.
The new girl, Indu, joined our class last week. She has heavy kajal, loud bangles, and she talks back to teachers in a way that makes everyone gasp. So on day one I told Ronit, "Trouble. You'll see. She'll be in the principal's office in a month." And every time she laughed in class I thought, see?
Today I lost my wallet in the canteen. It had my bus pass and the fifty rupees Papa gave me. I was panicking. Then Indu came up and handed it to me. "Found it under the bench. Count it." Everything was there.
I just stood there like a fool and said thanks. I had her figured out completely wrong, and I didn't even know her.
Mummy says a good son says sorry properly. Maybe Monday.
Vaibhav

qa.q: What was in Vaibhav's wallet?
qa.a: His bus pass and the fifty rupees Papa gave him.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel sure that Indu was trouble?
qa.a: Her kajal, bangles and way of talking back matched his idea of a troublemaker, so every laugh in class seemed to confirm it.

qa.q: What choice is Vaibhav thinking about for Monday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Saying sorry properly to Indu. It would mean acting on what he learned from what she did, not on his first judgement.

qa.q: How might Indu feel if she knew Vaibhav had called her trouble on day one?
qa.a: She might feel hurt or unsurprised, if people often judge her by her look, and his apology could mean a lot to her.

grounding: A teenage boy's diary shows he judged a new girl as trouble from her looks and speech, and was surprised when she returned his lost wallet.

passage:
Saturday, 2 a.m., hackathon, day 2
I picked the wrong team lead and I know it now.
Yesterday at the kickoff, Pankaj gave this amazing pitch: hands moving, jokes, words like "scalable" and "user journey." Everyone clapped. I thought, obviously he's leading, he sounds like someone who runs a startup. Salma, who sits next to me in the lab, said almost nothing. She just asked two quiet questions about the database. I didn't even think of her.
Now it's 2 a.m. Pankaj has been "networking" at the snack table for three hours. Salma has built the whole backend, fixed my login bug, and quietly written a task list on the whiteboard that everyone is following.
I think I confused sounding good with being good. I'm Hrithik, 20, supposedly smart, and I fell for a speech.
Tomorrow I'll suggest Salma presents the demo too.

qa.q: What has Salma built by 2 a.m.?
qa.a: She has built the whole backend.

qa.q: Why did it feel obvious to Hrithik that Pankaj should lead?
qa.a: Pankaj's confident pitch, with jokes and startup words, matched Hrithik's picture of a leader, so the style felt like proof of skill.

qa.q: What choice does Hrithik make for tomorrow, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Hrithik will suggest Salma presents the demo too, giving credit and visibility to the teammate whose work is actually holding the project together.

qa.q: How might Salma feel if she is asked to present the demo?
qa.a: She may be nervous about speaking up but pleased that her quiet, steady work has finally been noticed.

grounding: A student at a hackathon realises the team lead was chosen for a fluent, confident pitch while a quiet, more reliable teammate was overlooked.

passage: At the block office in Bhawanipatna, three people sat on the panel to hire teachers for the new village learning centres: Hemant, the programme manager, and two senior coordinators, Sarika and Irawati. Last year's best teacher, Sudhir, had come from the town college and spoke smooth English. By the fourth interview Hemant noticed a pattern. Whenever a candidate mentioned the town college or answered in English, Sarika's pen started moving fast. When a young woman from a nearby village answered in Kui and Odia, describing how she had run an evening class for twenty children, Irawati said, "Nice, but not like Sudhir." At tea, Hemant took a sheet of paper from his bag. "Can we agree what we're actually hiring for? Teaching children in their language, patience, attendance records. Let's each score those, one to five, before we talk." Sarika frowned, then nodded. The village woman's scores came out highest.

qa.q: Where did last year's best teacher, Sudhir, come from?
qa.a: Sudhir had come from the town college.

qa.q: What does Hemant seem to think as he watches Sarika's pen move fast?
qa.a: He seems uneasy, noticing that candidates who look and sound like Sudhir are being favoured whether or not they fit the actual job.

qa.q: What did Hemant propose at tea, and why did it work better?
qa.a: He proposed that each panellist score the real job needs, such as teaching in the children's language, patience and attendance, before discussing. That made them judge each person on evidence.

qa.q: How might the young woman from the nearby village have felt if the panel had not changed its method?
qa.a: She might have felt her real teaching experience counted for nothing because she did not resemble last year's star.

grounding: A programme manager in a small town notices a hiring panel favouring candidates like an earlier star, and proposes structured scoring.

passage: The bakery chain in Toronto was hiring four shift leads, and Tariq, the new operations manager, sat on the panel with Rosa from HR and a regional manager. Their best shift lead ever, Kevin, had been a college athlete, a tall, loud man full of energy. By Wednesday afternoon Tariq could see it: every candidate who played team sports got warm smiles and extra time. A quiet woman who had run a busy night shift at a hospital cafeteria for three years got twelve minutes and a polite goodbye. "She just didn't have that Kevin spark," Rosa said. Tariq didn't argue about spark. Instead he opened a laptop. "What if we list five things a shift lead actually does, like handling complaints, scheduling, stock, safety, training, and score each person on examples?" Rosa hesitated. "That's more work." "It is. But it's fairer." They re-scored the week's candidates that evening.

qa.q: How long had the quiet woman run a busy night shift at a hospital cafeteria?
qa.a: For three years.

qa.q: What does Rosa's comment about "that Kevin spark" suggest about Rosa's thinking?
qa.a: Rosa seems to be using Kevin as the picture of a good shift lead, so candidates who resemble Kevin feel right to Rosa, even if the job needs other skills.

qa.q: Which choice by Tariq helped the panel judge more fairly?
qa.a: Instead of arguing about spark, he listed five real tasks of a shift lead and asked the panel to score each person on examples.

qa.q: How might Rosa feel about the extra work of structured scoring?
qa.a: Rosa may feel a bit reluctant or defensive at first, but seeing the re-scored candidates side by side could help Rosa notice what had been missed.

grounding: A manager abroad notices his panel favouring candidates who resemble a past star, and proposes scoring everyone on real job tasks.
